_comment.manual: Texts for the Oddities chapter this mod adds to Forestry's own Forester's Manual. The entries themselves are JSON under assets/forestry/patchouli_books/foresters_manual/, because that is where Patchouli looks for that book's pages; the book is i18n, so every name and page text here is a translation key.
forestry_oddities.patchouli.category.odd: A short chapter of things I could not find anywhere else in this book, and so made myself: a frame that pretends to be the sun, a frame that carries a potion, and the parts that finally let you put a frame into an alveary and pay for its work with a wire.
forestry_oddities.patchouli.entry.odditi: Soft Light Frame

A hive that cannot see the sky will not work, and the only way round it used to be the gene for cave dwelling. I never liked breeding that in merely to put a hive in a cellar, so this frame does the job instead: while there is a charge in it, the bees under it work as if the sun were straight above them - in a cellar, under a hill, at the bottom of a mine.$(br2)It does nothing else. It will not make them quicker, it will not widen their range, and it will not touch their lives.
I set a redstone lamp into the window of a proven frame, held it in with two copper ingots and pegged it underneath with an iron one.

It is not free, and it does not arrive charged.$(br2)It will hold 1,000,000 FE, and every work cycle spends 80 FE of it. That is twelve and a half thousand cycles, or about four days of a hive that never idles. Charge it with anything that puts FE into an item; it has no way of giving the charge back. The cycle that spends the last of it still counts as sunshine, and after that the window goes dark and the bees stop until somebody charges it again. There is no durability on the frame at all, so no amount of work will ever wear it out.

Put it in any frame slot you have: one of the three in an $(l:forestry:beekeeping/apiary)apiary$(/l), or the single one that the $(l:forestry:oddities/alveary_frame_housing)frame housing$(/l) in this chapter gives an alveary. Unlike the frames you will have been using, there is nothing on it to wear away - what it costs you is the electricity, not the durability.
Infusion Frame

A frame is a set of promises: work faster, mutate more, live longer. This one takes its promises from a potion. Grind the potion into the frame and the effects of the potion become the frame's modifiers, while the duration of the potion becomes how long the frame lasts.$(br2)Which potion you choose decides everything about it, so no two of them are ever quite the same item.
Three sticks above, three below, blaze powder on either side, and any potion you like in the middle. Splash and lingering potions will do just as well.

A frame only cares about five of the things a potion can do.$(br2)Speed makes the queen work twice as fast for each level. Poison ages her ten times as quickly per level. Regeneration stops her aging altogether, and has the last word if the potion carries poison as well. Weakness makes mutations ten times as likely per level, and Water Breathing keeps the bees working in the rain.$(br2)By level I mean the level the potion itself shows. A potion carrying several of these effects grants every one of them.

How long the frame lasts is the duration of the potion in whole seconds: three minutes gives you a hundred and eighty uses, and a minute and a half gives ninety. It wears one point per work cycle, like any other frame, and breaks when the last point is gone. The window of the frame is tinted with the colour of the potion, in case you forget which was which in the chest.$(br2)A potion with none of those five effects makes a frame with nothing to say for itself, and a frame made with no potion at all has neither modifiers nor durability.
Alveary Frame Housing

For years this book has said that a frame cannot be stuffed into an alveary, and for years it has been true: the alveary has no slot for one. This part is my correction to my own writing - a wall block with a well in the middle of it, and the frame goes into the well.
An alveary block, ringed with sticks and cornered with planks.

Build it into the alveary the way you would a fan or a sieve: in place of one of the wall blocks of the bottom two layers, leaving the top layer plain.$(br2)Once the structure is whole, right-click the part and a single slot opens. Any hive frame will go in - the four Forestry ships, the two in this chapter, and whatever other mods have added - and nothing else will.

The frame speaks for the whole alveary from then on, and it is read afresh every time it is asked: put one in and it works, take it out and it stops. It wears one point per work cycle, exactly as it would in an apiary, though the $(l:forestry:oddities/soft_light_frame)soft light frame$(/l) pays 80 FE a cycle instead and never breaks.$(br2)The slot is saved with the part and drops out when the part is broken, and pipes and hoppers can reach it as well, if you would rather have a machine keep it fed.
Circuit Foundation

An alveary wall with a socket in it. Solder a board for the part - the $(l:forestry:core/soldering_iron)soldering iron$(/l) lists the layout as $(thing)Circuit Foundation$() - click it into the socket, and feed the part FE. While there is enough in the buffer to pay the board's bill, the programs on the board decide what the bees do next.
Two refined circuit boards and a golden electron tube along the top, redstone at the sides, three copper ingots along the bottom, and the alveary block in the middle.

Programming a board is the same job here as anywhere else. Take a $(l:forestry:core/soldering_iron)soldering iron$(/l), put a $(l:forestry:core/circuit_board)circuit board$(/l) and your electron tubes in it, and click the arrows until the layout reads Circuit Foundation. A basic board carries one tube and an intricate board four.$(br2)Click a finished board onto the socket. To get it back, click the socket while holding the iron, which costs the iron one point of durability. Only boards soldered in this layout will fit, and Forestry's machine boards are refused as well, while no pipe or hopper can reach the socket either way.

One tube is one program, and the ones that give numbers fall into two families.$(br2)For production there is the $(item)Iron Electron Tube$(), which makes the bees work half again as fast for ten FE a cycle, and the $(item)Diamantine Electron Tube$(), which makes them work two and a half times as fast for twenty. The $(item)Lapis Electron Tube$() does the same for flowering, at half again for ten. The $(item)Bronze Electron Tube$() stretches the working range to one and a half times for ten, while the $(item)Tin Electron Tube$() pulls it in to four tenths of that and knocks a tenth off the production besides, for the same ten.

The other numbers are about the queen and the air around her.$(br2)The $(item)Apatine Electron Tube$() gives her half again as much life for ten FE a cycle, and the $(item)Obsidian Electron Tube$() takes a fifth of it away for the same ten. The $(item)Golden Electron Tube$() makes mutations half again as likely for fifteen, and the $(item)Blazing Electron Tube$() heats the inside of the hive like the Nether for fifteen, so that a Nether bee will work anywhere at all.

The last five tubes have nothing to do with numbers. Each answers a question about whether a bee will work in a place at all, and no Forestry circuit I know of ever used one of them: the $(item)Copper Electron Tube$() keeps the rain off for ten, the $(item)Silicon Electron Tube$() gives a hive in a cave its daylight for fifteen, the $(item)Ender Electron Tube$() lets the bees work day and night for fifteen, the $(item)Amber Electron Tube$() dismisses temperature and humidity altogether for twenty-five, and the $(item)Emerald Electron Tube$() saves you a flower bed for thirty-five.$(br2)Two tubes answering the same yes-or-no question do not add up; two that give numbers do.

The part holds 1,000 FE and takes 500 from any offer, and can only be filled - nothing pulls the energy back out.$(br2)A work cycle of 550 ticks, twenty-seven and a half seconds, pays for the whole board at once, the sum of every program on it, so a cheap program cannot ride along on an expensive one: a board wanting 60 FE does nothing at 59. Every program also multiplies the genetic decay by one and a half, which makes a board of four five times the decay of a plain alveary. A circuit foundation is never free, however harmless its programs look.$(br2)Feed it from a $(l:forestry:oddities/alveary_transmission)transmission$(/l), or straight from a cable. Breaking the part drops the board, and the board itself never wears out.
Alveary Transmission

A part with no opinion about bees whatsoever. It takes FE in and hands it to the other parts of the same alveary, so that a wall full of circuit foundations needs one cable instead of one cable for every face.
Four copper gears in the corners, redstone along the edges, and the alveary block in the middle.

It holds 1,000 FE and takes 500 from any offer. Once a tick it hands out up to 500 FE, split evenly over the parts that can take it, and stops when it runs dry. It will not feed another transmission - the two of them would only push the same energy back and forth for ever.$(br2)It does nothing at all to the bees: no production, no range, no life. It has no screen of its own either, so right-clicking it opens the alveary's, and one that is idle and holding nothing costs nothing at all.
Alveary Ticker

The alveary works to a fixed count I have never been able to argue with: 550 ticks, one work cycle, twenty-seven and a half seconds. This part argues with it. It spends FE on extra ticks for the counter, and a powered alveary can be pushed all the way to one whole cycle per game tick.
A refined circuit board above and below, a clock on either side, and the alveary block in the middle.

Right-click the assembled part and a small instrument of a screen opens: a slider from x1 up to the housing's work throttle, with the multiplier and the cost beneath it. At x1 nothing happens at all, for it is an ordinary alveary. Pull the slider up and every extra tick of the counter costs ten FE, bought out of the part's own buffer and in whole ticks only: with 95 FE in it you get nine ticks and five FE back in change.$(br2)With no queen in the housing, or a princess still filling her place, it buys nothing, because there is no work cycle to be hurrying along. If something else changes the housing's throttle, the top of the slider moves with it.

The buffer is 20,000 FE and takes 10,000 from any offer, so a cable straight into the part will do, or a $(l:forestry:oddities/alveary_transmission)transmission$(/l) at a lower setting. At the top of the slider it spends 5,490 FE a tick, which empties a full buffer in about four seconds.$(br2)The clock on its sides turns at the setting: one turn every 1,280 ticks at x1, and one every 64 at the top.
